content: In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) maintained its recommendations for first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens for infants and children, as no newer, more effective, and tolerable options were available. Since then, dolutegravir (DTG) has been approved for children older than six years, and raltegravir (RAL) has been approved for use from birth, offering additional treatment options for neonates, infants, and children living with HIV. A raltegravir-based regimen may be recommended as an alternative first-line therapy for infants and children when approved dolutegravir dosing is unavailable. This recommendation is conditional and based on low-certainty evidence. An updated systematic review conducted in 2018 evaluated the efficacy and safety of dolutegravir in people living with HIV initiating first-line therapy. The review included 70 trials involving 33,148 participants randomized to 161 treatment arms. The analysis demonstrated highto moderate-quality evidence that a regimen of two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus dolutegravir was generally more effective than two NRTIs plus efavirenz (EFV) 600 mg for ART-naive adults. Dolutegravir showed higher rates of viral suppression, better CD4 cell count recovery, and a lower risk of treatment discontinuation. It also had superior viral suppression efficacy compared to other integrase inhibitors. Regimens containing dolutegravir and EFV 600 mg were comparable in terms of mortality, AIDS-defining illnesses, and serious adverse events. Dolutegravir offers additional advantages over EFV 600 mg, including a lower potential for drug interactions, a shorter median time to viral suppression, and a higher genetic barrier to resistance development. Its long half-life, low cost, and low dose make it feasible for inclusion in once-daily fixed-dose combinations. Dolutegravir also exhibits in vitro and clinical activity against HIV-2, which is naturally resistant to EFV. The availability of dolutegravir as a generic fixed-dose formulation and potential price reductions in lowand middle-income countries further support its use as the preferred option for initiating ART. However, dolutegravir has been associated with an increased risk of insomnia and neuropsychiatric adverse reactions, warranting further investigation. Current evidence does not suggest an increased occurrence of other serious adverse events, such as cardiovascular events, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, or suicidal behavior, in the short term. Identifying suitable regimens for adolescents is crucial due to their demonstrated risk of suboptimal adherence compared to adults, which increases their likelihood of treatment failure and drug resistance. In this context, more acceptable, tolerable, and forgiving regimens for adolescents are highly valued. Limited evidence exists on the effectiveness of dolutegravir versus EFV among adolescents. The Guideline Development Group endorsed extrapolating efficacy data from adult trials when direct comparative evidence for adolescents is unavailable. Clinical and programmatic experience with dolutegravir in lowand middle-income countries is limited, and its long-term safety remains unknown. A potential safety issue related to neural tube defects in infants born to women taking dolutegravir at conception has been identified from an ongoing observational study in Botswana. More data are needed on the safety and efficacy of dolutegravir at conception and among individuals receiving rifampicin for HIV-associated tuberculosis treatment. Programmatic assessments and clinical trials are underway to inform future policies. For neonates and children, the safety, tolerability, efficacy, and favorable pharmacokinetics of dolutegravir for children older than six years have been demonstrated in the short term. However, there is limited experience with dolutegravir use in children younger than six years. Preliminary pharmacokinetic data from an ongoing trial support using a simplified dosing approach of a 50-mg adult dosage for children weighing 25 kg or more. Similar to lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), dolutegravir overcomes the high level of pretreatment NNRTI resistance. A recent cohort study shows that dolutegravir achieves good viral suppression for children older than six years and weighing more than 15 kg and is safe and tolerable outside of a randomized controlled trial setting. Appropriate weight-based dosing for children younger than six years and weighing less than 15 kg is being identified, with approved dosing expected by late 2019. Dosing for HIV-associated tuberculosis treatment in children is still under investigation. The Paediatric Antiretroviral Drug Optimization group, an advisory group to WHO, has endorsed extrapolating efficacy data from adult trials when direct comparative evidence for children is unavailable. Unless a specific rationale exists, safety and pharmacokinetic data for children should remain the basis for considering new antiretroviral drugs for treatment guidelines for infants and children living with HIV. Due to the lack of comparative evidence between dolutegravir and the current standard of care in children (EFV for children older than three years and LPV/r for children younger than three years), data were extrapolated from adult studies. In adult data analysis, dolutegravir was superior to an LPV/r-based regimen in terms of viral suppression at 48 and 96 weeks, discontinuation, and emergent serious adverse events. For these reasons, the Guideline Development Group agreed that dolutegravir should be recommended as the preferred first-line regimen for children for whom approved dolutegravir dosing exists, although the certainty of the evidence was rated as low due to extrapolation from adult studies. As of mid-2018, dolutegravir can be used for children older than six years weighing at least 15 kg, with approved dosing down to four weeks expected by the end of 2019. Due to limited experience with dolutegravir among children, the Guideline Development Group also advised implementing routine active toxicity monitoring. For children for whom dolutegravir-approved dosing is unavailable, raltegravir is the only integrase inhibitor that can be used from birth. Approval of raltegravir was based on data from trials involving children that demonstrated appropriate pharmacokinetics, safety, tolerability, and efficacy of raltegravir for infants, children, and adolescents between four weeks and 18 years of age, as well as pharmacokinetics and safety data for neonates. Raltegravir successfully reduces viral load among infants with high viral load and is safe and well-tolerated for neonates and infants at high risk of infection. Its ability to rapidly reduce viral load makes it an appropriate candidate for first-line use among infants and young children for whom dolutegravir dosing is not yet available. Recent data support using raltegravir for children with HIV-associated tuberculosis infection receiving rifampicin-containing tuberculosis treatment. There is currently no direct evidence assessing the efficacy of raltegravir-based ART versus LPV/ror EFV-based ART among children living with HIV initiating treatment. Similar to dolutegravir, the Guideline Development Group extrapolated evidence from adult studies showing that raltegravir is superior to EFV and LPV/r in terms of viral suppression, with fewer people discontinuing due to adverse events and fewer serious adverse events. The certainty of the evidence was low because data were extrapolated from adults. Raltegravir and nevirapine (NVP) are currently the only treatment options for neonates. Because comparative evidence between raltegravir and nevirapine is lacking for neonates, extrapolation from efficacy studies involving adults is necessary. Based on data for adults, raltegravir in combination with an age-appropriate NRTI backbone is superior to an NVP-based regimen in terms of viral suppression and change in CD4 cell count. The differences were not statistically significant for any other outcomes. Despite its overall higher efficacy compared with the standard of care, raltegravir is known to have a lower genetic barrier to developing resistance compared with other integrase inhibitors. The Guideline Development Group raised concerns about the potential for suboptimal viral suppression and the risk of selecting for resistance to integrase inhibitors in the context of a partially active NRTI backbone resulting from pretreatment resistance to NRTIs, which has been documented in up to 20% of ART-naive infants and young children. Additionally, the WHO 2016 recommendation for using twice-daily administration of dolutegravir after failure of raltegravir-containing regimens makes using raltegravir less optimal in first-line ART unless no other effective options exist. For neonates, the lack of robust alternative options supports using raltegravir in first-line ART, as the risk–benefit balance differs from that for its use in older infants and children, who can use LPV/r solid formulations. For these reasons, the Guideline Development Group concluded that raltegravir for neonates should be preferred, whereas raltegravir can only be considered an alternative first-line regimen for infants and children until data for appropriate dolutegravir dosing become available. The Guideline Development Group noted that neonates starting ART with a raltegravir-based regimen should stay on this regimen for no longer than three months, as this is when they can transition to LPV/r solid formulations, to minimize selection for resistance to integrase inhibitors. For pregnant and breastfeeding women, pharmacokinetic data suggest that dolutegravir levels are relatively similar between pregnant and non-pregnant women, although they are lower during pregnancy than postpartum. However, dolutegravir levels appear to remain within therapeutic ranges during pregnancy. Dolutegravir has also been shown to transfer into breast milk, resulting in significant plasma concentrations among infants. The Guideline Development Group reflected on different sources of evidence for the possible teratogenicity of dolutegravir. Preclinical animal studies and early human clinical data on dolutegravir found no association with birth defects. However, a potential safety issue related to neural tube defects in infants born to women taking dolutegravir at conception has been identified from an analysis of an ongoing observational study in Botswana. This translates into a neural tube defect risk of 10 per 1000 women using dolutegravir compared with 1 per 1000 using other antiretroviral drugs. These data suggest that the potential safety issue might arise from a woman’s exposure to dolutegravir in the periconception period rather than during pregnancy. The same study had no other reports of infants with neural tube defects among women who started dolutegravir later in pregnancy, after the period of risk for developing neural tube defects (6–8 weeks after conception). To better understand this signal of potential risk, active research and surveillance are ongoing for additional pregnant women in Botswana and other countries where women have been exposed to dolutegravir at the time of conception. The incidence of other adverse birth outcomes associated with dolutegravir exposure during pregnancy—stillbirths, spontaneous abortions, preterm and very preterm delivery, small for gestational age, and very small for gestational age—are comparable to or lower than those reported for exposure to non-dolutegravir ART during pregnancy. Neonatal mortality does not differ significantly between infants born to mothers starting dolutegravir-based ART during pregnancy versus those starting EFV-based ART.
